record.paper_title: Dynamical criticality: overview and open questions
record.original_question: Can enforcing dynamical criticality, or properties correlated with it, serve as a general criterion for the automatic design of artificial systems such as learning systems, rather than relying only on ad hoc fitness functions tailored to specific tasks? The open problem is to determine whether the evolutionary advantages attributed to critical dynamical systems in nature can be translated into practical design principles for artificial systems and learning methods.

evidence.quote: A further issue that has not yet been discussed above concerns artificial systems: if critical dynamical systems have evolutionary advantages in nature, then this property may also hold for artificial systems, such as learning ones.
Therefore, enforcing dynamical criticality or correlated properties may provide a general criterion for the automatic design of such systems.
This would complement the usual approach consisting in defining ad-hoc and task dependent fitness functions in evolutionary techniques.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the design of artificial adaptive systems (for example, recurrent neural networks, reservoir computers, spiking networks, cellular automata, or Boolean networks used for learning tasks). A dynamical system is said to be at (or near) dynamical criticality if its parameters place it on the boundary between an ordered regime, where perturbations decay, and a chaotic regime, where perturbations grow exponentially; equivalently, the maximal Lyapunov exponent (or an analogous order parameter, such as the Derrida sensitivity for discrete systems) is close to zero, and observables typically display power-law correlations and a balance between robustness and flexibility.

Formulate and resolve the following design-principle question. Let 𝒮 be a parameterized class of artificial dynamical systems intended to perform learning or computation, and let 𝒞(s) be a quantitative measure of how close s ∈ 𝒮 is to dynamical criticality (or to a property strongly correlated with criticality, such as maximal dynamical complexity, vanishing Lyapunov exponent, or maximal mutual information between input history and internal state). Determine whether there exists a task-independent objective functional based solely on 𝒞 (and not on any task-specific fitness function) such that:

(a) optimizing 𝒞 over 𝒮 by an automatic procedure (e.g. evolutionary search, gradient descent, or self-organization) yields systems whose performance on a broad family of learning or computational tasks is competitive with, or superior to, systems obtained by directly optimizing task-specific fitness functions; and

(b) the evolutionary advantages attributed to critical dynamical systems observed in natural systems can be rigorously shown to transfer to such automatically designed artificial systems, in the sense of provable bounds (or strong empirical universality) relating proximity to criticality 𝒞(s) and task-general performance.

Equivalently: is dynamical criticality a viable, general-purpose, task-independent design criterion for automatically generating artificial learning systems, replacing or complementing ad hoc task-specific fitness functions?
artifact.status_search_result: The question remains an active research direction without a definitive resolution. Multiple recent works (edge-of-chaos initialization in deep nets, reservoir computing at criticality, mean-field tuning of spiking networks, neuromorphic nanowire networks, asynchronous critical systems) provide partial evidence that proximity to criticality enhances computational capacity and trainability, and propose automatic tuning schemes. However, no general theorem or universally accepted task-independent design criterion based solely on criticality has been established; criticality often requires fine-tuning and its universality as a stand-alone design principle is still debated.

status_evidence.title: Dynamical Criticality: Overview and Open Questions
status_evidence.snippet: Survey listing the use of criticality as a design principle for artificial systems among open questions.
status_evidence.claim: The question is presented as an open problem in the survey itself.

status_evidence.title: At the Edge of Chaos: Real-time Computations and Self-Organized Criticality in Recurrent Neural Networks
status_evidence.snippet: Networks perform complex computations on time series only near the edge of chaos.
status_evidence.claim: Partial empirical support that criticality correlates with computational performance, but not a general design theorem.

status_evidence.title: Avalanches and edge-of-chaos learning in neuromorphic nanowire networks
status_evidence.snippet: Edge-of-chaos dynamics enable optimal learning in neuromorphic hardware.
status_evidence.claim: Empirical evidence in specific hardware systems; not a general criterion.

status_evidence.title: A mean-field approach to criticality in spiking neural networks
status_evidence.snippet: Provides an analytical method to configure spiking networks near criticality, reducing online fine-tuning.
status_evidence.claim: Recent (2025) work still developing automatic-criticality-based design, indicating the question is active and not closed.

status_evidence.title: Revisiting the Edge of Chaos: Again?
status_evidence.snippet: Reassesses the edge-of-chaos hypothesis as a design principle for computation.
status_evidence.claim: The principle is still being debated and revisited rather than settled.
